content:
A couple of years ago I was giving a talk somewhere. I forget where exactly, but I remember what happened after because I let myself down.

I was pretty tired—it had been a long flight the day before and I was getting over a cold. I walked backstage and said thank you to the organizers and got ready to go.

“Could we take a picture?” they asked.

Of course, I said, thinking it was some kind of informal thing. It turns out they had a backdrop and wanted me to take a picture in front of their logo…and not just one picture but quite a few with quite a few people. Then they asked if I could wait a few minutes because there was someone else they wanted me to meet…and it was quite a few minutes…and then after I talked to them it turned out they also wanted to do a picture. Oh, let’s do a fun one too! And then, the videographer asked me if I could answer some questions for their podcast and record a testimonial. All the while they were also leading me towards a lunch with some of their clients that they were hoping I’d attend.

None of it was a huge imposition by itself, but it’s not stuff I normally agree to. I’m usually pretty good about saying “No” to things I don’t want to do—especially points that are usually, in the speaking world, points of a contract—but I was exhausted and I was alone and they were friendly. So it all kept adding up, along with my discomfort. What had started as a couple little things turned into basically a fleecing, they were using me for marketing materials and it was taking more and more time (all the while my flight was approaching).

In terms of things that have happened to me in my life, this was hardly the worst thing but when I got back to my hotel room to frantically pack and rush the airport, I couldn’t help but think: I could have stopped that at any point. Why didn’t I say something?

I’ve written a lot about the discipline of saying no. About how we have to get comfortable doing it, standing up for ourselves and protecting our time. About the giant “NO!” sign hanging in my office. About how “No” is a complete sentence. About not saying “maybe” when we really mean no. About how everything we say yes to is saying no to something else. About how we have to get comfortable disappointing people.

I know all this. I’ve practiced it. I’ve gotten much better at it. And yet there I was, following someone around, saying yes to thing after thing because I felt too uncomfortable to say no.

What happened?

This is something that the great Angela Duckworth addresses in her wonderful new book, Situated: Find the People and Places That Bring Out Your Best (we had a great conversation about it on the podcast). Yes, grit is important. Yes, discipline is a skill. Yes, we have to be able to do hard things. But we must also understand: behavior is situational. We’re not the same person in every situation. “The laws of physics are inescapable,” Angela told me. “So are the laws of psychology. And one of the laws of psychology is that we are reactive to our situation.”

Someone who is courageous one day, might not be on another. Someone who is hard to discourage in one area of their life, might be a quitter in another. Someone who is patient at work might be short-tempered at home. Someone who is outgoing around one group of people might be introverted around another. Someone who can say no easily in some settings might struggle to say it in others.

Why?

Because it depends!

It depends on what you ate for breakfast. It depends on how much sleep you got. It depends on your identity. It depends on who you’re around. It depends on where you are. It depends on whether it’s been a stressful day. It depends on so much!

That was one of the lessons I learned from that speaking event—the discipline of not putting ourselves in those situations in the first place. My team had not set me up to succeed. I had not set myself up to succeed.

The old ancient command, proclaimed by the Oracle at Delphi, was: “Know thyself.” “One must know oneself,” the philosopher and mathematician Blaise Pascal reminds us. “Even if it does not help in finding truth, at least it helps in running one’s life, and nothing is more proper.”

Knowing when you make good decisions and when you don’t is key. When you can trust yourself and when you can’t. When you need a buffer or a helper, and when you do better on your own. When you can handle the situation and when you need to get out of it.

Captain Arthur MacArthur—the father of Douglas MacArthur—was serving in New Orleans after the Civil War. There, a cotton broker trying to win the use of some army facilities left a large cash bribe in the hotel room of the young officer. MacArthur declined the bribe but afterwards, sent a telegram to Washington. “I request immediate relief from this command,” he told his superiors. “They are getting close to my price.”

What are your strengths? What are your flaws? What is your limit? Where are your buttons? What makes you tick? What is your Achilles’ heel? What tends to happen when you’re tired or hungry? What tends to put you in a bad mood? What tends to distract, rattle, or overwhelm you? “I tell my students,” Toni Morrison explained, “one of the most important things they need to know is when they are their best, creatively. They need to ask themselves, What does the ideal room look like? Is there music? Is there silence? Is there chaos outside or is there serenity outside? What do I need in order to release my imagination?”

“When are you at your best?” is a question we can apply to our working environments, to our routines and habits, to our information diets, to being a parent, a spouse, a boss, an employee, a friend, a teammate, a neighbor, a citizen.

When you are at your worst matters too. Noticing when my wife and I tend to argue or get frustrated with each other has been helpful not just in avoiding those spats but building a day/life around facilitating when we get along best. Noticing that I almost never get good writing done in the afternoons has been helpful too. Noticing that if I don’t work out in the mornings on the weekends, I tend not to be able to find the time to do it at all (or when I do, it’s a miserable slog) has meant that I fiercely protect that time.

You gotta know your weaknesses and make decisions so you can be strong. You gotta know what brings out your worst and arrange things so you can be at your best. You gotta know who you are not trying to be and set yourself to be who you are trying to be.

Behavior is situational. We are situational.

Which is why you gotta know thyself.

You gotta know the conditions that set you up for success.

You gotta know the people and places that bring out your best.

And your worst too.
